questions.stem:
A 55-year-old man has 2 months of cough, fevers and weight loss. A Gram stain of his sputum shows neutrophils and only faint, beaded, poorly staining structures that the technologist cannot call Gram positive or Gram negative. A second smear is stained with carbol fuchsin, heated, decolorized with acid alcohol and counterstained with methylene blue; it shows thin, slightly beaded rods that hold the fuchsia dye on a blue background.

Which property of this organism explains both staining results?
choices: A thick peptidoglycan layer that traps crystal violet after decolorization
A lipid-rich waxy wall of mycolic acids that resists both dye entry and removal
An outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharide that loses crystal violet
A polysaccharide capsule that excludes both stains from the cell surface
The absence of a cell wall, which leaves only the cell membrane to stain

explain.html:
Mycobacteria are technically Gram-positive rods, but they stain poorly on Gram stain because their thick, hydrophobic, waxy wall is full of mycolic acids. The same wall is the basis for the acid-fast stain: once carbol fuchsin is driven in (Ziehl-Neelsen with heat, or Kinyoun), the waxy wall holds it even through acid alcohol, so acid-fast bacilli look fuchsia (the classic red snappers) on a blue background.

The lecture notes that the mycolic acid wall also makes mycobacteria resistant to drying, and that a fluorochrome (auramine-rhodamine) stain, which binds mycolic acids, is about 10 times more sensitive than the carbol fuchsin stain.
why: A thick peptidoglycan layer explains ordinary Gram positivity, not acid fastness.
Lipopolysaccharide belongs to Gram-negative organisms and does not explain acid fastness.
Mycobacteria are identified by their wall, not a capsule.
Organisms without a cell wall do not retain carbol fuchsin.
explain.takeaway: The mycolic acid-rich waxy wall makes mycobacteria stain poorly on Gram stain and retain carbol fuchsin after acid alcohol (acid fast).
explain.topic: Mycobacterial cell wall and acid-fast staining
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 71-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has a chronic cough. She was born in the United States and has no known TB exposure. Three sputum specimens are sent. Two show a few acid-fast bacilli on smear. A nucleic acid amplification test (Xpert MTB/RIF) on the first specimen is negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and a repeat on the second specimen is also negative. Cultures are pending.

Which of the following is the most likely interpretation of these results?
choices: Smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis that the nucleic acid test has missed
Pulmonary tuberculosis caused by a strain resistant to rifampin
A false-positive smear caused by contamination with stain precipitate
A nontuberculous mycobacterium rather than M. tuberculosis
Contamination of the sputum with dead tuberculosis organisms

explain.html:
A positive acid-fast smear shows mycobacteria but cannot tell M. tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM). The NAAT is specific for M. tuberculosis and has a good negative predictive value in respiratory samples with enough organisms to be smear positive.

The lecture's rule: if the NAAT is negative while the smear is positive, the presumptive diagnosis is NTM. Her bronchiectasis and lack of TB risk fit, since NTM pulmonary disease is now more common in the US than pulmonary TB. Culture will identify the species.
explain.table:
SmearNAATPresumptive reading
PositivePositiveMTB (over 95% positive predictive value)
NegativePositiveMTB
PositiveNegativeNTM
NegativeNegativeTB not excluded, but infectivity low
why: When enough organisms are present to be smear positive, the NAAT rarely misses M. tuberculosis.
Xpert detects M. tuberculosis regardless of rifampin resistance, and it was negative.
Two separate specimens were smear positive, which argues against an artifact.
Dead M. tuberculosis would still make the NAAT positive.
explain.takeaway: A positive AFB smear with a negative TB NAAT points to a nontuberculous mycobacterium; a positive NAAT, even with a negative smear, points to M. tuberculosis.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 46-year-old man who keeps a large home aquarium has had a slowly enlarging, painless nodule on the back of his right hand for 6 weeks. New nodules have since appeared in a line up his forearm. He recalls scraping the hand while cleaning the tank. Biopsy shows granulomas, and an acid-fast stain shows a few bacilli. Culture at the lower temperature requested by the lab grows a mycobacterium after 2 weeks. His wife asks whether she could catch it from him.

Which of the following is true of this organism?
choices: It is a member of the tuberculosis complex and spreads by droplet nuclei
It lives in the environment and is not passed from person to person
It grows within 7 days on routine bacterial media as a rapid grower
It requires a human reservoir and passes between household members
It cannot be cultured and is diagnosed only by skin biopsy appearance

explain.html:
A hand nodule after a scrape while cleaning a fish tank, with lymphatic spread up the arm, is the lecture's classic association for Mycobacterium marinum, a slower-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM).

NTM are ubiquitous in water and soil, form biofilms at water and surface interfaces, and have no human or animal reservoir, so there is no person-to-person transmission. This contrasts with the M. tuberculosis complex, which has human reservoirs and spreads through the air, which is why TB is a public health concern and NTM disease is not.
why: The TB complex has human reservoirs and airborne spread; this is an environmental NTM.
It took 2 weeks to grow, which fits a slower grower, not a rapid grower.
NTM have no human reservoir.
It grew in culture; the non-cultivatable mycobacterium in the lecture is M. leprae.
explain.takeaway: Nontuberculous mycobacteria live in water and soil and do not spread person to person; M. marinum is linked to fish tanks.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Over 3 months, six patients who had cosmetic surgery at the same outpatient center develop draining wound infections that fail to improve on cephalexin. Routine bacterial cultures grow long, filamentous Gram-positive rods within 5 days, first dismissed as contaminants. An acid-fast stain of the wound drainage shows long, beaded, filamentous acid-fast rods. An inspection finds that instruments were rinsed in tap water after sterilization.

Which organism group is most likely responsible?
choices: Slow-growing Mycobacterium avium complex
Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
The non-cultivatable Mycobacterium leprae
Pigmented slow growers such as M. kansasii
Rapid-growing nontuberculous mycobacteria

explain.html:
Rapid-growing NTM (for example M. abscessus, M. chelonae and M. fortuitum) grow in under 7 days on solid media and can even grow on routine bacterial media, where they look like filamentous Gram-positive rods. On acid-fast stains they look atypical: longer and more filamentous than the small beaded rods of M. tuberculosis.

They live in water, and the lecture lists clusters of surgical wound infections as one of their disease associations. Tap water rinsing of instruments is the shared source here.
why: MAC is a slow grower, mainly a lung or disseminated pathogen, and would not grow in 5 days.
M. tuberculosis is a slow grower that takes weeks and does not cause instrument-linked wound clusters.
M. leprae cannot be cultured at all.
M. kansasii is a slow grower.
explain.takeaway: Rapid-growing NTM grow in under 7 days, can appear on routine bacterial media as filamentous Gram-positive rods, and cause clusters of surgical wound infections.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 49-year-old man with alcohol use disorder and poor nutrition is started on a single drug for latent TB infection that blocks synthesis of a lipid unique to the mycobacterial wall. He was not given any supplement with it. After 2 months he reports burning and tingling in both feet that is slowly rising up his shins. His liver enzymes are mildly elevated. He has taken the drug as prescribed.

Which of the following would most likely have prevented his new symptom?
choices: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) given with each dose
Folic acid given with each dose
Monthly visual and color vision testing
Taking each dose with a high-fat meal
Monthly measurement of serum uric acid

explain.html:
A single-drug latent regimen that inhibits mycolic acid synthesis is isoniazid (INH). Its two main toxicities are hepatitis (mild chemical hepatitis is common, clinical hepatitis is rare, and risk rises with age, alcohol and chronic liver disease) and a dose-related peripheral neuropathy.

The neuropathy is prevented by giving vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH, which the lecture writes as INH plus B6. Malnourished patients and heavy drinkers are among those most at risk, so this patient should have received it from the start.
why: Folic acid does not protect against INH neurotoxicity.
Visual monitoring is for ethambutol optic neuritis.
Food does not prevent neuropathy.
Uric acid monitoring is for pyrazinamide, not INH.
explain.takeaway: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and causes hepatitis and a peripheral neuropathy that vitamin B6 prevents.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 57-year-old man starts four-drug therapy for culture-proven pulmonary tuberculosis. After 3 weeks he develops sudden severe pain, swelling and redness of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of his left foot. Joint aspiration shows needle-shaped crystals. Serum uric acid is 10.4 mg/dL (normal 3.5 to 7.2). His clinician considers stopping the responsible drug but worries about how that would change the length of his treatment.

Stopping the drug most likely responsible would have which effect on his treatment?
choices: It would lose activity against organisms in the central nervous system
It would leave the regimen unable to block mycolic acid synthesis
It would remove the drug that hedges against isoniazid resistance
It would lose the drug that shortens the total course to 6 months
It would remove the only drug in the regimen that is bactericidal

explain.html:
Gout with a high uric acid in a patient on standard four-drug therapy points to pyrazinamide (PZA), which raises uric acid and causes gout and arthralgias. PZA is active against semi-dormant organisms inside cells at acid pH, and adding it gives faster sterilization.

When rifampin and PZA are both given during the 2-month initial phase, the total course can be 6 months. Without PZA in those 2 months, the minimum duration rises to 9 months.
why: CNS penetration is not the reason PZA is valued in the regimen; ethambutol is the drug with poor CNS penetration.
Mycolic acid synthesis is blocked by isoniazid.
Ethambutol is the hedge against isoniazid resistance.
Isoniazid and rifampin are also bactericidal.
explain.takeaway: Pyrazinamide raises uric acid and can cause gout; given with rifampin in the first 2 months it shortens TB treatment to 6 months.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 64-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease has been on four-drug therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis for 7 weeks. Her drug doses were never adjusted for her kidney function. She reports blurry vision in both eyes and says that colors have started to look washed out. Visual acuity has dropped from 20/20 to 20/60 in both eyes. Fundus examination is normal.

Which drug is most likely responsible, and why was she at higher risk?
choices: Isoniazid, because it is metabolized by hepatic acetylation
Rifampin, because it induces cytochrome P450 enzymes
Ethambutol, because it is cleared by the kidneys
Pyrazinamide, because it raises the serum uric acid
Rifabutin, because it accumulates in the lens of the eye

explain.html:
Loss of visual acuity and color discrimination on TB therapy is retrobulbar (optic) neuritis from ethambutol, a dose-dependent toxicity. That is why patients on ethambutol have their visual acuity and color vision monitored.

Ethambutol is cleared by the kidneys and needs dose adjustment in renal insufficiency. Without adjustment, her levels rose and so did the risk of this dose-related effect. Ethambutol inhibits cell wall synthesis and is usually bacteriostatic.
why: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, not optic neuritis.
Rifampin causes drug interactions, orange fluids, rash and flu-like illness.
Pyrazinamide causes hyperuricemia and gout, not vision loss.
Rifabutin does not cause this optic picture.
explain.takeaway: Ethambutol causes dose-dependent optic neuritis (acuity and color vision loss) and is renally cleared, so its dose is adjusted in kidney disease.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 39-year-old man with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and a large cavity on chest radiograph completes a 2-month initial phase of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol under directly observed therapy. His isolate is fully susceptible. He feels better, but the sputum culture collected at the end of the 2 months still grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. The team is planning his continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampin.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: Stop all drugs, because a full 2-month initial phase has been completed
Continue isoniazid alone, since the organisms are now in the dormant phase
Restart the same four drugs from day 1 for another 2-month initial phase
Switch to a second-line regimen because the culture shows drug resistance
Continue isoniazid and rifampin for a longer continuation phase

explain.html:
Standard therapy is a 2-month initial phase of four drugs followed by a 4-month continuation phase of isoniazid and rifampin, for 6 months in all. The goal of the continuation phase is durable cure, meaning no relapse after therapy stops.

Some patients have a higher risk of relapse after the shorter course, and the lecture names cavitary disease plus a sputum culture still positive at 2 months as a main reason to give a longer continuation phase. His isolate is susceptible and he took his drugs under observation, so the plan is to extend isoniazid and rifampin, not to change drugs.
why: The continuation phase is still needed to eradicate persisting organisms.
Single-drug therapy is never used for TB disease.
Repeating the initial phase is not the response; the continuation phase is extended.
His isolate is fully susceptible, so there is no resistance to act on.
explain.takeaway: TB disease is treated with a 2-month initial phase of RIPE then isoniazid and rifampin; cavitary disease with a positive 2-month culture earns a longer continuation phase.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman from Bangladesh has a positive interferon-gamma release assay found on employment screening. She has no symptoms, and her chest radiograph is normal. She drinks alcohol daily and has chronic hepatitis C with mildly elevated liver enzymes. She takes no other medications. Her clinician agrees that the benefits of treating her latent infection outweigh the risks and wants the regimen least likely to injure her liver.

Which regimen is most appropriate?
choices: Isoniazid daily for 9 months
Isoniazid daily for 6 months
Rifampin daily for 4 months
Rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol
Pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months

explain.html:
Latent TB infection is treated with a single drug or two drugs. The preferred regimens are 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, 4 months of daily rifampin, and 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampin; 6 or 9 months of isoniazid alone are alternatives.

Isoniazid hepatitis is the main safety concern on latent treatment, and its risk rises with age, alcohol, chronic liver disease and other liver toxins. Rifampin alone avoids isoniazid, is preferred, and is shorter. Drug interactions are the main concern with rifampin, and she takes no other medications.
explain.table:
LTBI regimenRank
3HP: isoniazid plus rifapentine once weekly for 3 monthsPreferred
4R: rifampin daily for 4 monthsPreferred
3HR: isoniazid plus rifampin daily for 3 monthsPreferred
6H or 9H: isoniazid for 6 or 9 monthsAlternative
why: Nine months of isoniazid carries the most isoniazid liver exposure.
Six months of isoniazid still carries isoniazid hepatitis risk in a woman with liver disease and alcohol use.
Four drugs are for TB disease, not latent infection.
This is not a latent treatment regimen, and pyrazinamide is itself hepatotoxic.
explain.takeaway: Preferred LTBI regimens are 3HP, 4R and 3HR; in someone at high risk of isoniazid hepatitis, rifampin alone avoids isoniazid.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 31-year-old woman with multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis is started on an all-oral 6-month regimen that includes linezolid, pretomanid and a diarylquinoline. The diarylquinoline was the first drug developed and approved specifically for MDR TB. Her team orders a baseline electrocardiogram and plans repeat tracings during therapy, along with liver tests.

The diarylquinoline acts on which target, and what is the reason for the ECG monitoring?
choices: Mycolic acid synthesis, because it can cause heart block
Bacterial RNA polymerase, because it can cause bradycardia
ATP synthase, because it can prolong the QT interval
NADH dehydrogenase, because it can cause atrial fibrillation
DNA gyrase, because it can cause ventricular hypertrophy

explain.html:
Bedaquiline, a diarylquinoline, inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, a site of action unique to antimycobacterial agents. It was the first drug developed and approved for MDR TB and is part of the 6-month bedaquiline, linezolid and pretomanid regimen.

Its toxicities in the lecture are QT prolongation, hepatotoxicity, nausea and arthralgias, so the ECG is checked before and during therapy. The other targets belong to other agents: isoniazid (mycolic acid), rifamycins (RNA polymerase), clofazimine (NADH dehydrogenase) and fluoroquinolones.
why: Mycolic acid synthesis is the isoniazid target.
RNA polymerase is the rifamycin target.
NADH dehydrogenase is the clofazimine target.
DNA gyrase is the fluoroquinolone target.
explain.takeaway: Bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, is used for MDR TB, and prolongs the QT interval.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old man from Peru is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis after sputum smears and a nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) are positive. The NAAT reports no rifampin resistance mutation. He starts a standard four-drug regimen. After 6 weeks his cough has improved, and a resident proposes repeating the NAAT to show that the organisms have been killed, and canceling the cultures since the diagnosis is already confirmed.

Which of the following is the best response to this plan?
choices: Keep the cultures, which are needed for full drug susceptibility testing
Cancel the cultures, since the NAAT already excluded drug resistance
Repeat the NAAT, since a positive result will show rifampin resistance
Repeat the NAAT, since a negative result will confirm a cure
Cancel the cultures, since smears can track susceptibility

explain.html:
The NAAT detects mycobacterial DNA, whether the organisms are dead or alive. It can stay positive after organisms are no longer viable, so a positive NAAT should not be repeated and cannot track response to treatment.

Xpert MTB/RIF also detects only most rifampin resistance mutations. A result without a rifampin mutation says nothing about isoniazid or the other drugs, and molecular tests do not detect every resistance locus. That is why a positive NAAT still needs cultures: growth is required for phenotypic susceptibility testing to every drug in the regimen.
why: Xpert tests rifampin resistance mutations only, not resistance to the other drugs.
A positive NAAT on therapy could reflect DNA from killed organisms, not resistance.
The NAAT detects DNA from dead organisms too, so it cannot confirm cure.
Smears count organisms but give no susceptibility information.
explain.takeaway: A TB NAAT detects DNA from viable or dead organisms and only most rifampin mutations, so it is not repeated to monitor therapy and cultures are still needed for susceptibility.
explain.topic: Limits of NAAT and the need for culture
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a kidney transplant on a calcineurin inhibitor for rejection prevention is diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis. She is started on four drugs, one of which turns her urine and tears orange. Two weeks later her calcineurin inhibitor level has fallen well below target despite unchanged dosing, and her creatinine is rising. The transplant team asks which TB drug could replace the culprit while keeping the regimen effective.

Which of the following is the best choice?
choices: Rifabutin, a rifamycin with less effect on drug-metabolizing enzymes
Rifapentine, a longer-acting rifamycin given once weekly
Ethambutol at a higher dose to make up for the lost rifamycin
Isoniazid at a higher dose to make up for the lost rifamycin
Pyrazinamide for a full 9 months in place of the rifamycin

explain.html:
Orange body fluids identify rifampin. Rifampin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (encoded by rpoB) and is the most important first-line drug, but it strongly induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and P-glycoprotein transport. That lowers the levels of many co-administered drugs, here her calcineurin inhibitor, which threatens her graft.

The lecture's solution is rifabutin, which has less enzyme-inducing effect and can replace rifampin, so she keeps the benefit of a rifamycin. Rifapentine is still a rifamycin inducer, and dropping the rifamycin class entirely would weaken the regimen and lengthen therapy.
why: Rifapentine is also a rifamycin that induces drug metabolism.
Ethambutol is mostly static and cannot replace the most important first-line drug.
Isoniazid is already in the regimen and cannot replace a rifamycin.
Pyrazinamide adds its benefit together with rifampin, not as a replacement for it.
explain.takeaway: Rifampin induces cytochrome P450 and P-glycoprotein and lowers levels of many drugs; rifabutin induces less and can replace it.
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
Two patients are seen in a TB clinic on the same day. Patient 1 is an asymptomatic 25-year-old with a positive interferon-gamma release assay and a normal chest radiograph, who is started on a single drug. Patient 2 is a 50-year-old with a large right upper lobe cavity and smear-positive sputum, who is started on four drugs. A student asks why giving Patient 2 a single drug would be unsafe when it is acceptable for Patient 1.

Which of the following best explains the difference?
choices: Single drugs cannot penetrate a cavity, but they penetrate granulomas well
Patient 2's organisms are already resistant, while Patient 1's organisms are not
Combination therapy is used in disease to reduce toxicity by allowing lower doses
A cavity holds enough organisms that resistant mutants are present before therapy
Latent organisms are replicating faster and are killed before mutations can arise

explain.html:
Resistance arises from spontaneous chromosomal mutations at a low, fixed rate (around 1 in 10 million to 100 million organisms for isoniazid and 1 in 100 million to 1 billion for rifampin). A cavity can hold up to 100 billion organisms per milliliter, so mutants resistant to any one drug are almost certainly present before treatment starts. A single drug would kill the susceptible majority and select the resistant mutants.

Resistance to two drugs at once requires both mutations in the same organism, about 1 in 1015, so a combination regimen prevents this. In latent infection the organism count is low (under 10 million) and not actively replicating, so the risk of selecting resistance with a single drug is low.
why: Penetration is not the explanation; the size of the organism population is.
Nothing indicates Patient 2's strain is resistant; the concern is mutants within a large population.
TB regimens combine drugs to prevent resistance, not to lower doses.
Latent organisms are few and not actively replicating.
explain.takeaway: TB disease is always treated with drug combinations because large bacillary populations contain spontaneously resistant mutants; low-burden latent infection can be treated with one or two drugs.
explain.topic: Why combination therapy for disease but not LTBI
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old man from Moldova presents with 3 months of cough and weight loss. He was treated for pulmonary tuberculosis 5 years ago, took his pills irregularly without observation, and stopped after 3 months when he felt better. Sputum smear is positive, and a nucleic acid amplification test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis with a rifampin resistance mutation. Later culture-based testing shows resistance to rifampin and isoniazid and susceptibility to fluoroquinolones.

Which of the following best describes his tuberculosis?
choices: Mono-resistant TB acquired at the time of his first infection
Multidrug-resistant TB that was most likely acquired during therapy
Extensively drug-resistant TB that was most likely acquired during therapy
Pre-extensively drug-resistant TB acquired at the time of his first infection
Drug-susceptible relapse with a false-positive molecular resistance result

explain.html:
Resistance to at least both isoniazid and rifampin defines multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB. Pre-XDR adds fluoroquinolone resistance, and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB adds resistance to other key drugs as well; his isolate is fluoroquinolone susceptible, so it is MDR.

Primary resistance means a person was infected with a resistant strain; secondary (acquired) resistance develops during treatment. Prior treatment that was irregular, unobserved and stopped early, now relapsing, is the classic setting for acquired resistance and one of the lecture's main reasons to worry about MDR, along with contact with an MDR case and failure to respond to standard therapy. This is why directly observed therapy is used.
why: He is resistant to two drugs, not one, and his history points to acquired resistance.
XDR requires fluoroquinolone resistance plus other key drugs; his isolate is fluoroquinolone susceptible.
Pre-XDR requires fluoroquinolone resistance.
Culture-based testing confirmed the resistance, so it is not a false-positive molecular result.
explain.takeaway: MDR TB is resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampin; irregular, unobserved prior treatment is the main setting for acquired resistance.
explain.subject: Microbiology
